questions: Did these movements begin suddenly, within seconds or minutes?
Do you also have new weakness, numbness, difficulty speaking, facial drooping, vision loss, severe imbalance, or confusion?
Have you had a severe or unusual headache, loss of consciousness, or a seizure with this?
Do you have diabetes, or have you recently had very high blood sugar?
Have you recently started, stopped, or changed a medication or recreational drug, especially an antipsychotic, anti-nausea drug, stimulant, anticonvulsant, or levodopa?
Have you had a recent head injury, brain infection, fever, or cancer?
Are you pregnant, recently postpartum, or taking estrogen-containing medication?
Have you ever had similar movements before, or do close relatives have similar involuntary movements?
Are the movements present during sleep?
Do they disappear completely when you are asleep?
Have you had a recent sore throat or other infection followed by joint pains, rash, or abnormal movements?
Do you have a history of stroke, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, atrial fibrillation, or other vascular disease?

results: 1. Full bedside neurological examination, including mental status, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination, reflexes, gait, and characterization of the involuntary movements
mental status / cognitive screen: progressive disorientation, tangential speech, grandiose hallucinations and euphoric affect
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): hemichorea affecting one side
distribution of the movements (one side, both, face, limbs): not characterised
effect of voluntary action and anxiety: no clear change
effect of sleep: movements stop in sleep
3. Non-contrast CT scan of the head
CT head (non-contrast): symmetric frontal-predominant atrophy, no focal lesion
4. CT angiography of the head and neck
5. MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted, FLAIR, susceptibility-weighted, and contrast-enhanced sequences
brain MRI with contrast: 1.5T with gadolinium - frontal-predominant atrophy but NO focal lesion, with normal basal ganglia structure and volume
6. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, and thyroid-stimulating hormone
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
7. Coagulation studies, including prothrombin time/INR and activated partial thromboplastin time
8. Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring
10. Fasting lipid profile and hemoglobin A1c
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Huntington disease due to a pathogenic CAG-repeat expansion in the HTT gene

ALTERNATIVE 1: Autoimmune encephalitis, particularly anti-NMDA-receptor encephalitis

ALTERNATIVE 2: Wilson disease

ALTERNATIVE 3: Sporadic Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (Heidenhain/extrapyramidal presentation)
